title: Detection of Obtain Capabilities
summary: This detection strategy covers the resource development phase of obtaining capabilities, the parent activity of buying, downloading, or building tools, exploits, and payloads for later use. It matters because capability acquisition is the point where an intrusion stops being an idea and starts producing artifacts that touch your estate, such as reconnaissance tooling, cloud instances, or a command and control service. The telemetry that makes detection possible is proxy and resolver logs for tool download sites, cloud provider audit logs for new subscriptions and instances, endpoint records for new administrative tools, and threat intelligence reporting. The main failure mode is that the same tools are used legitimately every day, so the rule must anchor on who is getting them and where they came from, not on the tool name alone.

beginner.definition: This detection looks at the broad step where an attacker gets the tools and code needed for an attack. A capability is any tool, exploit, or program that helps the attacker do their work. The rule watches for the download and use of such tools from unusual places at unusual times. It also watches for new cloud accounts and servers that appear for no clear business reason.
beginner.whyItMatters: Capabilities must be obtained before they can be used. That makes this a good moment to act, because the attacker has not yet reached your valuable data. The same tools are often reused in many campaigns, so shared clues help everyone. Watching the acquisition also warns you which stage of an attack may come next.
howItWorks: The web proxy and DNS logs show downloads from tool hosting and code sharing sites.
Cloud audit logs show new subscriptions, instances, or storage buckets in an account.
Endpoint records show new administrative or network scanning tools on a host.
The SIEM joins these sources by user, host, and time. Threat intelligence adds context.
The rule scores the event against the user role and normal download history.
A standard user obtaining attacker tooling, or a new cloud resource with no owner, raises an alert.
beginner.example: Think of a workshop store cupboard with a sign out book. Every borrowed tool gets a name, a date, and the borrower. One visitor takes a cutting tool, a mask, and a drill in a single visit. That visitor never works in the workshop, so the foreman asks a question. The sign out book is our proxy and cloud log.
takeaways: Anchor on the user, the source, and the role, never on a tool name alone.
Cloud audit logs catch infrastructure that attackers rent before they use it.
This phase is broad, so expect to run several smaller rules instead of one large rule.

objectives: Describe the obtain capabilities phase and why it is worth monitoring.
Name telemetry sources that record tool, exploit and infrastructure acquisition.
Write a rule that scores tool downloads against the user role.
Explain how cloud audit logs reveal pre attack infrastructure.
Discuss how to keep legitimate administrative tool use out of the alert queue.
dataSources: Web proxy logs recording downloads of executable or archive files with destination domain, user agent and request size
Recursive DNS resolver logs for queries to tool hosting, code sharing and paste service domains
Cloud provider audit logs for new subscriptions, instance creation, key pair creation and storage bucket creation
Endpoint process creation records for network scanning and credential dumping tools with their parent process and user
logic: The pattern is a user, host, or cloud account acquiring tooling that is inconsistent with its normal role or its history, especially tooling that supports scanning, exploitation, or remote control. The fields that must be correlated are the requesting identity, the host, the destination domain or service, the file name and hash of what was retrieved, the parent process that launched it, and the time related to the change calendar. The malicious case is a standard user account downloading a scanning tool from a personal cloud drive and running it during the working day from a temporary directory. The benign case is the security team pulling approved assessment tooling from an internal share during a scheduled test.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Acquisition of Administrative or Attack Tooling by a Standard User
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   service: proxy
# detection:
#   selection:
#     cs-uri-extension:
#       - 'exe'
#       - 'zip'
#       - '7z'
#       - 'ps1'
#   filter_approved:
#     r-dns|contains:
#       - 'internal-share[.]example[.]com'
#       - 'approved-vendor[.]com'
#   condition: selection and not filter_approved
# level: medium
falsePositives: Developers who download build tools and packaged runtimes from public code hosting sites
Information technology staff who fetch administrative utilities from vendor support portals
Security analysts who pull assessment tooling from an internal repository during an approved test window
tuningNotes: Build a per user and per host baseline of download destinations and file types, then filter approved vendor portals, internal shares, and package repositories used by development teams. Scope the rule to standard user accounts and to hosts outside the engineering and security groups, and add a separate scoring path for privileged accounts so you still see their activity at lower priority. The coverage you lose is an attacker who compiles or writes the tool locally, which produces no download at all, so pair this rule with the capability development rules.
